articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a mandatory vaccination and COVID-19 testing policy for all employees. All city employees – fulltime, part-time, volunteers and interns – must report their vaccination status to the city’s Human Resources Department. This includes City Councilmembers and those serving on city commissions. To be considered fully vaccinated, 14 days must have passed since an employee received the final dose of a two-dose vaccine (Moderna or Pfizer), or a dose of a one-dose vaccine (Johnson and Johnson). The proposition was discussed at the most recent City Council meeting on September 7, at the request of Mayor Teddy Gray King. “There is a moral imperative to move forward with this [mandate],” Mayor King said. Unless excused through an approved accommodation request, all employees must comply with the requirement to be fully vaccinated, and vaccination and reporting requirements would be a minimum qualification for new hires. Failure to comply could result in termination. articles.text: Accessible voting locations open as of Sept. 11 The recall election of Gov. Gavin Newsom is on Tuesday, September 14. Local election offices, including the Alameda County Registrar of Voters, sent out mail ballots for the Gubernatorial Recall Election on August 16. A recall procedure has been part of the state’s political system since 1911 and provides a mechanism for the public to attempt to remove elective public officials from office before the end of their term. At least 1,495,000 valid petition signatures, or 12% of the votes cast for the office of Governor in 2018, were received. Democrat Gov. Newsom is the second California governor ever to face a recall election. Five attempts to recall the governor have failed to qualify for the ballot since he took office in January 2019. Gray Davis was removed from office in 2003, only the second state governor successfully recalled in U.S. history. He was replaced by actor Arnold Schwarzenegger. All registered voters received a ballot in the mail. If you are a resident of Alameda County, you can verify your registration address and voter status by visiting www.acvote.org/mvp. The county is also offering a new way for voters to track and receive notifications on the status of their vote-by-mail ballot, powered by “BallotTrax” - interested residents may visit www.acvote.ballottrax.net to The vote-by-mail packet will contain your ballot card, a return envelope, instructions for returning your ballot, and an “I Voted” sticker. While the county is encouraging mail-in voting due to the current health pandemic, safe and accessible in-person voting options will be available. Accessible voting locations will be open starting Saturday, September 11. Voters may drop vote-bymail ballots in the ballot box located on Highland Way near the mailboxes 24 hours a day, up to and including Election Day. The Veterans’ Memorial Building serves as an Accessible Voting Location. Any resident of Piedmont or Alameda County can come to the Veteran’s Hall and cast their ballot or drop off a vote-by-mail ballot. The culture is still tribal and so a woman like our Syrophoenician is considered even lower than children because she is an outsider. In Jewish customs outsiders and women were considered unclean. Here is a woman pleading for her daughter to be healed and Jesus is kind of rude. We usually like to think of Jesus as all loving, but even he is a bit flawed in this passage in his treatment of the woman. He uses the term “dog” to give her status as lower than children. This woman doesn’t give up though. She hears Jesus’s reference to her and cunningly says, “Sir, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” Imagine how humble this woman had to be to accept her place. articles.text: The Piedmont Planning Commission will consider new wireless communication facilities design standards and listen to comments from the public at its meeting on Monday, September 13. Wireless communication facilities in Piedmont include telecommunication towers such as the Crown Castle distributed antenna system installation, and the Gulf South Towers cell facility in the Public Works corporation yard. At the meeting, city staff will present an informational report on the status of the draft amendment to the Piedmont Design Guidelines to establish design standards for the facilities. The goal of the standards is to ensure all facilities are integrated within existing and new infrastructure, while having a limited impact on Piedmont’s built and natural environment. The intention of the design standards is to provide a user-friendly document for “both professionals and the general public alike to understand Piedmont’s preferred standards for WCF,” an accompanying staff report stated. The September 13 meeting will be the Planning Commission’s first review of the proposed amendments to the Piedmont Design Guidelines, as well as the first public comments. The Planning Commission will not take action at the meeting. Public hearings will be scheduled later this fall for both the Planning Commission and City Council. Commissioners and members of the public may submit comments on the draft standards in writing by October 4 to provide adequate time for revision. articles.text: Piedmont School District accepted a grant from PG&E for six electric vehicle charging stations, as confirmed by the school board on August 25. The stations will be installed in the parking lot next to the John Morrison gym and high school band room. The PG&E grant is being offered to school districts throughout the state. PG&E will pay for all charging station infrastructure and costs to maintain the equipment for eight years. Piedmont School District will pay for the charging station electrical usage on a separate bill at a lower rate than currently paying. The value of the grant is estimated at approximately $300,000. After eight years, ownership of the stations can be transferred to the District. PUSD can also request the removal of the stations. Priority use for the charging stations will be given to electric vehicles owned by the district. It currently has three electric vehicles being charged at its Maintenance Building. The District also owns nine gas-powered vehicles, and plans to replace some of these with electric vehicles sometime in the future. The charging stations may also be used by school district staff to charge their privately owned EVs. Staff members will use a phone application to pay for the electricity used and those funds will be applied to the District’s electricity bill. “Now that the project is approved, the plan will be put together and submitted to the Division of the State Architect for approval,” said Communications Director Brian Killgore. No timetable currently exists for approval, installation or project completion. The school district moved on this offer quickly, in comparison to the City which has rejected a free installation offer from PG&E and East Bay Community Energy. The city council has been offered four charging stations for Bonita Avenue, but the proposal has been rejected twice over concerns of limited parking in the city center. PUSD has accepted a grant from PG&E to install six electric vehicle chargers in the parking lot next to the John Morrison gym.
articles.title: School district accepts PG&E grant for 6 EV charging stations

Wireless communication facilities in Piedmont include telecommunication towers such as the Crown Castle distributed antenna system installation, and the Gulf South Towers cell facility in the Public Works corporation yard. At the meeting, city staff will present an informational report on the status of the draft amendment to the Piedmont Design Guidelines to establish design standards for the facilities. The goal of the standards is to ensure all facilities are integrated within existing and new infrastructure, while having a limited impact on Piedmont’s built and natural environment. The intention of the design standards is to provide a user-friendly document for “both professionals and the general public alike to understand Piedmont’s preferred standards for WCF,” an accompanying staff report stated. articles.text: During the August 25 Piedmont School Board meeting, board members conducted a cursory discussion on potentially requiring students to present proof of vaccination to attend school. A volunteer survey about student vaccine status was sent on August 24 to all parents with students aged 12 and older. Culver City School District became the first in the state of California to announce the requirement that students 12 and older must be vaccinated to attend their public school in West Los Angeles. Culver City announced its intent on August 19 for families to have proof of vaccine by November 19 to attend school. “I am very much in favor ofmandating student vaccine, I don’t think it is an easy decision. We do open ourselves us to exposure for litigation, and that is something the board will have to weigh versus student health,” said Superintendent Randy Booker. Booker favors a wait and see plan, contrary to forging ahead like Culver City. “For the most part, districts are waiting, [to see] who is going to be the first, to then learn from that and develop policy from that,” said Booker. “I think...you are not going to be able to do stuff if you are not vaccinated in a few months,” said Board member Hilary Cooper. “For the greater good, we should do that. “If we need to say ‘if you can’t provide proof of vaccination, go ahead and be tested once a week,’ absolutely,” she stated. “Hands down, without hesitation, I have a strong belief in a vaccine policy. When there are Pfizer and Moderna have been working since March 2021 on clinical trials of the COVID-19 vaccine for young people age 5 and older. all the FDA approvals, I believe we should require vaccination requirements for everyone on campus, whether a learner or a teacher,” added board member Amal Smith. All board members, including Cory Smegal, Veronica Thigpen and Megan Pillsbury, publicly expressed their support for a mandate. The voluntary survey about student vaccination status (of those eligible 12 and older) has received a quick response from parents. The survey was sent to 1,385 students in grades 6-12 on August 24. As of September 7, more than 1,000 responses have been received. The content of the responses has not been revealed, Booker will announce survey details at the next board meeting, Tuesday September 14. Merely collecting the information from the voluntary survey lets District nurses determine who can remain in school following a possible exposure, who must quarantine and for how long and what follow up testing is required,” explained the district’s Communications Director Brian Killgore. Currently, there is no mandate for a COVID-19 vaccine or requirement to submit vaccination status at the district, and there is no state-wide mandate for vaccinations as the basis of enrollment in public schools. Piedmont School District will consider issues of health exemptions and fall-backs, possibly including weekly testing for those who don’t provide proof. On August 23 the Pfizer vaccine was upgraded from emergency approval to full FDA approval for those age 16 and up. Emergency approval of the Pfizer vaccine allows for those 12-15 to receive the vaccine. Pfizer and Moderna have been working on clinical trials for kids age 5 and older since March this year. According to Pfizer’s website, it expects to receive full FDA approval for the vaccine to be given to youth aged 12-15 and emergency approval for children aged 5-11 in October.

pages.text: Wednesday, September 8, 2021 7 School Board considers vaccine mandate for students By Jay Russell During the August 25 Piedmont School Board meeting, board members conducted a cursory discussion on potentially requiring students to present proof of vaccination to attend school. A volunteer survey about student vaccine status was sent on August 24 to all parents with students aged 12 and older. Culver City School District became the first in the state of California to announce the requirement that students 12 and older must be vaccinated to attend their public school in West Los Angeles. Culver City announced its intent on August 19 for families to have proof of vaccine by November 19 to attend school. “I am very much in favor ofmandating student vaccine, I don’t think it is an easy decision. We do open ourselves us to exposure for litigation, and that is something the board will have to weigh versus student health,” said Superintendent Randy Booker. Booker favors a wait and see plan, contrary to forging ahead like Culver City. “For the most part, districts are waiting, [to see] who is going to be the first, to then learn from that and develop policy from that,” said Booker. “I think...you are not going to be able to do stuff if you are not vaccinated in a few months,” said Board member Hilary Cooper. “For the greater good, we should do that. “If we need to say ‘if you can’t provide proof of vaccination, go ahead and be tested once a week,’ absolutely,” she stated. “Hands down, without hesitation, I have a strong belief in a vaccine policy. When there are Pfizer and Moderna have been working since March 2021 on clinical trials of the COVID-19 vaccine for young people age 5 and older. all the FDA approvals, I believe we should require vaccination requirements for everyone on campus, whether a learner or a teacher,” added board member Amal Smith. All board members, including Cory Smegal, Veronica Thigpen and Megan Pillsbury, publicly expressed their support for a mandate. The voluntary survey about student vaccination status (of those eligible 12 and older) has received a quick response from parents. The survey was sent to 1,385 students in grades 6-12 on August 24. As of September 7, more than 1,000 responses have been received. The content of the responses has not been revealed, Booker will announce survey details at the next board meeting, Tuesday September 14. Merely collecting the information from the voluntary survey lets District nurses determine who can remain in school following a possible exposure, who must quarantine and for how long and what follow up testing is required,” explained the district’s Communications Director Brian Killgore. Currently, there is no mandate for a COVID-19 vaccine or requirement to submit vaccination status at the district, and there is no state-wide mandate for vaccinations as the basis of enrollment in public schools. Piedmont School District will consider issues of health exemptions and fall-backs, possibly including weekly testing for those who don’t provide proof. On August 23 the Pfizer vaccine was upgraded from emergency approval to full FDA approval for those age 16 and up. Emergency approval of the Pfizer vaccine allows for those 12-15 to receive the vaccine. Pfizer and Moderna have been working on clinical trials for kids age 5 and older since March this year. According to Pfizer’s website, it expects to receive full FDA approval for the vaccine to be given to youth aged 12-15 and emergency approval for children aged 5-11 in October. articles.text: The second annual Walk for Wellness, the largest fundraiser for Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center, will take place September 20 through 26. It is an inclusive and socially-distanced event open to the entire Piedmont Community, and funds raised allow the Center to maintain a robust training program to meet the needs of Piedmont students. The Wellness Center was established by Piedmont Middle School Counselor Brooke Zimmerman in 2007 and offers individual and group counseling services to address a myriad of common adolescent concerns, as well as crisis intervention and referrals to community mental health services. The Wellness Center also covers a majority of Individualized Education Program (IEP) based counseling at the middle and high schools. According to the Wellness Center Support Committee, which organizes the fundraiser, one quarter of middle school students and one third of high school students seek counseling or other services from the Center each year. Beyond the services provided, the Center also serves as a muchneeded respite area for students. Students can use the waiting room, have tea, read materials and resources provided, and simply relax. “We are so appreciative of our Parent Support Committee, which raises this money for us. Primarily, these funds go to support stipends for our unlicensed staff, who are accruing hours toward licensure under supervision of the clinical supervisors,” explained Alisa Crovetti, a Clinical Supervisor for the Center. The first Walk for Wellness event raised $37,000 in funds, allowing the Center to attract high-quality candidates and increase retention. “We have therapists returning for multiple years, which greatly enriches the quality of our services,” Crovetti said. The Wellness Center has a partnership with the UC Berkeley Psychology Internship Consortium, which allows them to hire pre-doctoral interns. Interns hold graduate training in psychological assessment and psychotherapy, usually one year out of completing their Ph.D. Financial support for the Center last year allowed Clinical Supervisors to provide training on teletherapy, solution-focused therapy, anti-racist and culturally-sensitive mental health approaches, and Dialectical Behavior Therapy, which Crovetti said is a “preferred modality for students who have trouble regulating their emotions, coping with stress, and maintaining stable relationships.” Crovetti also noted that, despite the challenges brought on by the pandemic, teletherapy or “remote” therapy has become a preferred modality even when in-person services are available for some clients. “At the beginning [of 2020], we provided a two-part training on teletherapy – laws and ethics related to providing teletherapy with minors and also the clinical implications and skills associated with it,” added Crovetti. “In spring, we transitioned to a hybrid approach, which allowed some services on site and the remainder via teletherapy.” Crovetti said that she recognizes the unique challenges facing students this year as they return to school in the midst of a global pandemic. Funds raised from the Walk for Wellness will place the Center in a good position to address these concerns, primarily by hiring and retaining stellar personnel. “Many students are feeling a lot more anxiety than is typical with the return to school. Many of them have experienced social isolation during the last year, and it feels overwhelming to be back with so many students,” she said. “The funding, very importantly, allows us to maintain a robust training program for our unlicensed therapy staff.” Piedmonters are encouraged to gather their friends and family members and participate in as many walks as possible during the week of September 20. You can post photos from your walk on Instagram by tagging the handle@Piedmont-wellness. To register and make donations, visit: www.piedmontwalkforwellness.org, or email piedmontwalkforwellness@gmail.com.

articles.text: Screens have become a much bigger part of our lives since the start of COVID-times, and I’m pretty sure we aren’t the only family with that story. So, before the school year started, we made a family decision. It was time to detox. We discussed our options and decided unanimously that we needed a full stop – one week with no screens (with one exception: Baking Shows, but only if the whole family was watching). Here is what I noticed in this week-long, screen-free time. Creativity thrived My two youngest have very active imaginations, and my oldest really likes building and making things. So, we prepared for the week by making space for imagination play. What if they couldn’t think of anything to do? They could always go outside and play imagination games. My oldest used some of his Bar Mitzvah money to buy a remote-control car kit that he could build. As the week progressed, we created art projects and new games as well. We talked more I really enjoy chatting with my gang. They have really interesting thoughts on lots of different topics. What we noticed in our week with no electronics is that they were willing to “practice the art of conversation” at dinner with a lot more patience than if they had the option of returning to their video games. Age divide diminished I looked into the living room early on and saw that the 13-yearold, 10-year-old and 5-year-old were all actively engaged in some wrestling game where the two little ones were trying to get their big brother to roll off the carpet. Everyone was laughing and having fun. This happened throughout the week. In contrast, when they are in Screen Land, it is hard for them to find anything that all three can agree on to watch or do together because they are all interested in different kinds of content. Families can get more creative when they have more time away from computer screens. They were more present We spent a lot of time noticing things during the week. Seeing beautiful vistas on walks, really recognizing the flavors in foods, noticing how the people around us were feeling. I asked my gang about this, and they all recognized that they were more present and not thinking about “what comes next” nearly as much. More physical activity My kids are pretty good in terms of moving their bodies; they all have sports they enjoy and are very happy to go on hikes or bike rides. But, if given the option to sit and stare at a screen for hours on end, they will do just that. I was thrilled that, for screen-free week, they were constantly moving. We were lucky enough to have access to a pool, so they spent hours jumping in and out of the water, but even when they were not in the pool, they were flipping over couches, running around the kitchen island, jumping up and down in the driveway. They were in constant motion...until about 2 p.m. each day, when my 5-year-old crashed and took a spontaneous nap in the middle of the living room. There was more space for being silly Perhaps the most fun of all was that there was just more time and space for silliness. One of the joys of raising kids is being able to share in the silly that comes so naturally to them. But, when they have screens as an option, the silly just diminishes. They are spending more time in their own little bubble, and, let’s face it, silly is more fun when you share it. There were dumb dad jokes from my husband, wacky faces, tickle fests and even a few homemade riddles. All together, it made for more laughter and a lot of smiles. Now that school is back in our lives, we will go back to the “no electronics during the week” rule that existed pre-COVID, but I’m excited to continue the conversation with my kids about weekends. They noticed the changes too. I think we are in a strong position to find a better balance. Every family is different, so this might not be right for yours, but I think it was an interesting experiment. So many of us are struggling with the shift back to “normal,” even though things still aren’t normal. I hope you are finding interesting experiments with your children too. We were lucky enough to have access to a pool, so they spent hours jumping in and out of the water, but even when they were not in the pool, they were flipping over couches, running around the kitchen island, jumping up and down in the driveway. They were in constant motion...until about 2 p.m. each day, when my 5-year-old crashed and took a spontaneous nap in the middle of the living room. There was more space for being silly Perhaps the most fun of all was that there was just more time and space for silliness. One of the joys of raising kids is being able to share in the silly that comes so naturally to them. But, when they have screens as an option, the silly just diminishes. They are spending more time in their own little bubble, and, let’s face it, silly is more fun when you share it. There were dumb dad jokes from my husband, wacky faces, tickle fests and even a few homemade riddles. All together, it made for more laughter and a lot of smiles. Now that school is back in our lives, we will go back to the “no electronics during the week” rule that existed pre-COVID, but I’m excited to continue the conversation with my kids about weekends. They noticed the changes too. I think we are in a strong position to find a better balance. Every family is different, so this might not be right for yours, but I think it was an interesting experiment. So many of us are struggling with the shift back to “normal,” even though things still aren’t normal. I hope you are finding interesting experiments with your children too. articles.text: Photos by Brian Mahany Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany (not pictured) are now 4-1 as a duo and have won all four matches in straight sets. The Piedmont High girls’ tennis team took a one-sided 7-2 loss to non-league North Coast Section opponent Miramonte in Orinda on Thursday, September 2. They returned home to take on Alameda on Tuesday, September 7, but lost to the Hornets 6-1. Miramonte competes in Division 1 of NCS, while Piedmont plays in Div. 2, making the two sides eligible for play nine matches (six singles and three doubles). Alameda is the first league opponent Piedmont has faced this fall. “Miramonte always has a strong team, but it’s good to play tough teams early in the season. Alameda was a really, really tough loss; things certainly could’ve gone the other way. I’m looking forward to seeing them again later in the season,” explained coach Jim Landes. Miramonte loss Among the victories was No. 1 singles starter Bridgette McEfee claiming her first win of the season, defeating Riley George in three sets, 6-1, 5-7, 10-7. Also in the win column was the No. 1 doubles pair of Amanda Becker and Audrey Mahany, defeating Ellie Foster and Sophia Kan in straight sets; 6-1, 7-5. Bridgette McEfee won her first match of the season against Miramonte, 6-1, 5-7, 10-7. Miramonte won all but one of the remaining matches in straight sets. In singles, Anne Jumper lost 7-6 (7-3), 6-2 at No. 2; Michaela Bini had a close 7-5, 6-4 loss at No. 3; Anika Gilliland fell 6-3, 6-2 at No. 4; freshman Emma Eisemon lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 5; and Cecilia Defazio lost 6-0, 6-0 at No. 6. In doubles, No. 2 Mara LaForte and Rose Seimers had a three-set loss that went to a third set super breaker, 6-7 (7-2), 6-1, 10-7. At No. 3, Audrey Frankel and Sofia Ferraro lost 6-1, 6-4. articles.text: Skyline Lacrosse, founded in 1979 and the premiere youth lacrosse program in the area, is set to host boys and girls camps at Coaches Field every Sunday in two separate sessions starting September 12 through December 12. The camps are designed for boys and girls in Under-8, U10, U12 (middle school) and U14. The camps are focused on student-athletes looking for their first experience in the sport. “Typically we have fall ball where we try to get kids excited about playing in the spring. We want to get kids who have never played the sport before to come to our training sessions and learn the game,” said Carlton Chan, a longtime coach at Skyline, and Piedmont High School head women’s coach for the past four years. “This gets kids who have never played the game more comfortable with lacrosse.” Chan will help coach the camp’s U14 players. Skyline Lacrosse is one of the oldest lacrosse organizations in California, having a clear impact on boys’ and girls’ lacrosse throughout the nearby high school programs. For years, Skyline helped players reach varsity rosters at Piedmont, Bishop O’Dowd, Berkeley, Miramonte, and Castro Valley. “Skyline has always built itself as a recreational program, so it is open to everybody. There are no barriers to entry in comparison to a lot of privately run, for-profit clubs. I think that grassroots-effort is what has built its reputation. The purpose of the camps is getting kids who have never played the sport,” said Chan. The camps will be focused on players looking for their first lacrosse experience. Skyline competes in the Northern California Junior Lacrosse Associate, which oversees all clubs from the Bay Area, from Monterey to Sacramento. “These sessions will be focused on fitness, fundamentals, and basic teamwork. Fitness will be a big component; kids go into spring ball really out of shape so we’re going to preach the basics of fundamentals, avoiding injuries, and building their conditioning. We’re going to give them the tools to take what they learn from us and develop their own workout plan in regards to lacrosse,” explained Chan. As much fun as they are having, the results show on the field. Piedmont High’s 2019 NCS Championship winning girls’ team, 2019 WACC Champion, and 2018 WACC Championship winning girls’ teams were nearly completely Skyline alumni, just one player “The NCS championship winning team was all Skyline alum,” recalled Chan. Aside from the interested potential Piedmont student-athlete looking to get a leg-up on cracking the varsity roster, the camp is open to students from all schools. Skyline has alums currently on varsity teams at Bishop O’Dowd and Berkeley, in addition to Piedmont. Skyline camps will be $190 for U8 and U10 boys and girls, and $255 for U12 and U14 players. For more information, visit www.SkylineLacrosse.com or contact Skyline Administrator Joe Reid at Admin@skylinelacrosse.com. Boys will have U8, U10, U12, and U14 teams.

articles.text: PHS looks ahead to season-opener this Friday. Sept. 10 It’s been a rough start to the fall season for Piedmont’s football team. It’s first two contests have been canceled, most recently a scrimmage with Encinal on September 3 that was canceled by North Coast Section officials who ruled that Encinal had already completed a regular season game and was ineligible to play in a separate scrimmage. “The North Coast Section commissioner [Pat Cruickshank] canceled the scrimmage. NCS rules states a team cannot scrimmage twice in a season. Encinal has already had an official scrimmage and a game, so they informed us that the Jets couldn’t play,” explained Piedmont coach Jerome Johnson. This comes after the varsity team watched numbers drop to under 20 athletes. A scrimmage on Friday, August 27 at Miramonte was canceled at the last minute due to poor air quality. The Highlanders will enter the game this Friday with Durham without having had any d scrimmages or practice games. The varsity’s only competition has been with its own junior varsity team. “It’s tough going into a game without having any controlled time,” said Johnson. It’s an unfortunate turn for the football program after going 5-0 last season and finishing as Staff Photo Witter Field was empty on Friday, September 3 after the scrimmage with Encinal was canceled by NCS commissioner Pat Cruikshank. the top-ranked NCS Division 5 school. Despite Piedmont’s 100 years of history with a successful football program, the team has been the hardest hit program this fall. “We’re not the only one in the same boat,” said Athletic Director Bradley Smet. “There are a lot of schools with impacted numbers, and the pandemic could be part of the reason. A lot of schools have smaller numbers, but football has definitely taken a hit.” “Some kids just decided not to come out. We’ve had some players who were on the team last year, but this year either they were less enthusiastic or parents voiced concern about them playing football specifically,” added Johnson. Both Varsity and Junior Varsity will now look ahead to its season-opener this Friday against Durham High School outside Chico, a school with an enrollment of 350 students. It will be the first meeting in football between the two schools. The Trojans are currently 1-0 with a 14-8 win over Williams HS and finished 4-2 last season, 3-7 in 2019, and 11-2 in 2018 when they won the Sacramento Valley Athletic Association championship. Friday’s game at Witter Field starts at 7 p.m., with the JV game at 4:30 p.m. PHS looks ahead to its official home-opener at Witter Field this Friday, September 10 against Durham at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Alisa Golden’s “Nature on Loan,” an exhibition of art quilts, continues at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Sunday and next, September 19. Gallery hours are from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., and there will be a walk-through tour with the artist this Sunday, September 12, at noon. Golden’s background in creative writing, printmaking, and book arts offers a unique starting point for her work in textiles. The expansive exhibition showcases her work in printing, painting, beading and stitching. The quilts, art and poetry are inspired by “natural themes addressing our relationships and responsibilities, from the California fires and the pandemic, to botanicals and birds,” the artist said. “As a printmaker and writer, I am fascinated with marks and traces and how they become symbols for and signs of the people and beings who were there before. Each piece functions as a page where I can print from linoleum blocks, photopolymer plates or type, and then embroider and Artist Alisa Golden quilt a longer text or texture,” Golden said. “The photographic possibilities for solar printing from my own photographic imagery and hand-dyeing techniques appeal to me as well. I like the space between images and words, the colors and titles, where the viewer must interpret or fill in the gap, a little mysterious leap of inference.” The artist works in many sizes, and most quilts on display are for sale. You can contact Golden directly at info@neverbook.com. No reservations are required for admission to open gallery hours, and all county COVID-19 guidelines will be observed. The festival has drawn more than 10,000 art and nature enthusiasts to Lake Merritt since 2012. The festival is celebrating its 10th anniversary over three nights, October 14 through 16. Guests will experience 60 locally-produced illuminated art displays spread throughout the seven-acre municipal gardens. There will also be a kids’ “ fun zone,” art market, food court, and a beer and wine garden. All festival attendees must provide proof of vaccination or a negative COVID test to enter. This outdoor concert and socially distant show will feature an unconventional orchestra performing on the beautiful lawn in front of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The Renegade Orchestra describes itself as “throwing out all the old conventions of a quiet, sleepy, stuffy show of musicians locked in straight jackets of tradition.” The ensemble features a The Renegade Chamber Orchestra will perform outdoors at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, September 11, at 12 noon. set of virtuosic orchestra musicians and a hard-driving rhythm section. “Our music pushes a lot of boundaries of what an orchestra can do,” said conductor Jason Eckl. “Although they are boundary-pushing, the music is familiar and more toe-tappin’ rock and roll than you normally find in an orchestral setting.” The program of music includes works from diverse composers such as Nina Simone, Miles Davis, the Mamas and the Papas, and Donna Summer. “We all love the classical traditions, but now it’s time to let our hair down,” said Renegade cellist Rebecca Roudman. articles.text: The U.S. Conference of Mayors adopted a resolution urging Congress to provide arts and culture relief funding in the wake of the COVID pandemic. The initiative was led by San Francisco Mayor London Breed and Chicago Mayor Lori Lightfoot. The Conference of Mayors is an official, non-partisan organization of cities with populations of 30,000 or more and comprises 1,400 cities across the nation. In collaboration with the San Francisco Arts Alliance, the mayors reinforced federal policy recommendations to address the “the urgent needs of the nation’s arts and culture sector, and to take prompt and coordinated action to integrate arts into [the nation’s] recovery and revitalization efforts.” “Our arts and cultural institutions are the lifeblood of our vibrant communities and essential to our economy,” Mayor Breed said. “The arts define us as a city, they create jobs, and they are paramount in bringing together our diverse communities as we push for equity across all institutions. As we continue on this path of economic recovery, it has never been more critical to invest in the arts.” The arts and culture sectors contributed more than $877 billion to the nation’s economy in 2017, according to the San Francisco Arts Alliance. The current losses sustained by the sector as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic have reached $15 billion as of August this year. The Alliance seeks to lobby legislative issues which impacts the arts and culture community on local, state, and federal levels in order to ensure the equitable recovery of San Francisco. The Conference of Mayors is urging relief that will extend the Employment Retention Tax Credit beyond 2021 and modify nonprofit eligibility.

articles.text: The just released film is an epic, sea-faring tale, adapted from the 2000 best-selling non-fiction book by Nathaniel Philbrick. Set in 1819-20 during a period when the whaling industry was robust and sperm whale oil kept the lights burning and the wheels of the still nascent industrial revolution turning. Initially set in Nantucket, the film tells the story of the Essex, captained by the inexperienced George Pollard (Benjamin Walker), who was reluctant to turn to his first lieutenant, Owen Chase (Chris Hemsworth), fearful that he would seem weak. It was estimated that the journey of the Essex would last some one to three years, depending on how long it took to fill its holds with 2,000 barrels of oil. After a year at sea and little oil to show for it, Chase and Pollard are told of an area off the southern coast of South America said to be superb hunting. The information comes with a grim caveat: there is a massive whale out there that will, without hesitation, ram a ship and breach its hull. Discounting the story, the Essex sets sail south by southwest, headed for the hunting grounds described. The film opens with a writer, Herman Melville, hoping to convince one of the survivors, Tom Nickerson (Brendan Gleeson), then a young cabin boy (Tom Holland) serving on the Essex, to tell him the story of the whale and the sinking of the ship. At first reluctant to reveal any details to Melville, Nickerson finally relents. In a series of long flashbacks, he shares the story while Melville painstakingly takes notes. The essence of the tale is not just about the whale – 100 feet long, barnacle-encrusted, battered and covered with white spots – but of the men’s survival in their lifeboats for 90 days. In the Heart of the Sea is not about a singular man’s obsession with a white whale, which was Melville’s fictional account, published in 1851, later titled Moby Dick. Rather, it’s about the men of the Essex and what they endured after they sat and watched their ship burn and then sink beneath the horizon, knowing they were thousands of miles from land. Director Ron Howard also injects into the movie the 19th century reality that the whale oil industry was a lucrative business that required the harvesting of the largest mammals on earth, purely for profit. The tension between the exploitation of the earth’s resources for profit is still a conundrum some 195 years later for which we still have not found a balance. In the Heart of the Sea. Starring Chris Hemsworth, Brendan Gleason and Ben Whishaw. Directed by Ron Howard. 2 hrs., 1 min. Rated PG-13. Cillian Murphy, Benjamin Walker and Chris Hemsworth in In the Heart of the Sea. articles.text: Sam Elliott stars in The Hero. This may sound a bit hyperbolic, and Sam Elliott would likely reject the praise out of hand, using some purple language that would seem completely in character, but the fact is, as an actor, Elliott is a national treasure. He possesses not only that easily recognizable, sonorous voice, but he is also the last of a type, that cowboy who rode across a red dirt plain, stacked Colorado pillars in the distance, the sun at his back, ever alone. After decades wearing worn western garb Elliott has merged with that mythic image that we carry with us when we think of the Old West. Granted that may never have been, but there it is. In this movie we see Sam Elliott, lean as a weathered fence post, his 71 years etched in the crevasses of his leathery, tanned face, his frame all angles, his persona to a fault laconic, often sardonic. In The Hero Elliott plays the role of Lee Hayden, a man holding his regrets at bay with alcohol and weed, still able to scratch out a living making voice-over commercials for the likes of Lone Star Barbecue Sauce. This film finds a sweet spot and manages to stay there because of Elliott’s ability to never let his character slip in the realm of the maudlin, even when he gets some medical news that gives him bridled pause. Suddenly his life is derailed, and his estrangement from his daughter, Lucy (Krysten Ritter) and ex-wife, Val (Katherine Ross, Elliott’s real wife), give his very brief contact list kept on his phone a new urgency. He also meets a far younger woman, Charlotte (Laura Prepon), who makes him realize that he is at the beginning of the end of his life (no matter the medical diagnosis), and that his self-centered halcyon days are gone. He now finds himself standing alone on a beach gazing at the horizon. Though the story is as spare as Elliott’s grin, this is never a vanity film. This is Elliott at his best, and as Lee, he refuses to turn away from who he has become, a man filled with life still, but a life constantly tempered by a sense of loss. Some of the moments in “The Hero” are sublime. Others are filled with an abiding melancholy. Perhaps melancholy is how you ultimately define growing old, each day slipping through your grasp like so many grains of desert sand, each night given over to restless sleep, always confronting what was and will never be again. The Hero. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Sam Elliott, Laura Prepon, Katherine Ross. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated R. ®

articles.text: A scene from Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Like its predecessor, Peter Rabbit, Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway is a computer-animated hybrid, based on the much-loved books by Beatrix Potter. Kids love this rabbit, and The Runaway has an energetic, wack-a-mole, convoluted plot, set in great part in London and not the familiar Windemere farm. The story opens with the marriage of Beatrix (Rose Byrne) and Thomas (Domhall Gleeson), who, due to the efforts of Bea, are now living in relative harmony with the farm animals, most especially Peter (James Corden) and Thomas, whose trust of Peter is still a work in progress. Bea and Thomas have been working on a series of books that feature tales about the denizens of the McGregor farm. They receive a letter in the mail from a London publisher Nigel BasicJones (David Oyelowo). He wants to take Bea’s charming local stories commercial, a proposal that causes some concerns for the couple. But out of curiosity and to put to rest their questions about the methods to be used by Nigel, they take a meeting in London with the publisher, bringing with them not only Peter, but the whole crew: Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki), Cotton Tail (Aimee Horne), and cousin Benjamin (Colin Moody). Peter, as it turns out, is not happy about the way he is portrayed in the stories, characterized as a bit of a rogue; Nigel refers to him as a “bad seed,” even villainous. So, in a pique, he leaves the group, only to hook up with some bad company, headed up by a rabbit named Barnabas (Lennie James). And so begins a series of adventures that take Peter first to Barnabas’ hideout where he learns that there’s a plan afoot to carry out a vegetable heist from the local farmers market. As it turns out, their carefully formed plans turn into a mess. Peter and his clan get swept up by the Pet Pound, then freed, and head back to the farm where Peter seeks out the help of Thomas. They plan to return to London and defeat the underhanded work of Barnabas. Peter Rabbit 2 is exciting, slapdash, and even prankish, much to the delight of the kids who are happily watching events unfold, with tight corners gotten into and, of course, gotten out of. It’s all a lot of fun and the real-life animation is once again superb. Peter Rabbit 2: The Runaway. Directed by Will Glick. articles.text: Monsters, Inc. has a wonderful premise that will resonate with kids of all ages. I mean, what youngster hasn’t woken up in the dark night, the house asleep, and peeked over the covers at the closed closet door and imagined what might be behind it. “Was that a sound? Did I hear a creak from across the room?” Pixar, masters of computer animation and wonderful storytellers, offers a boisterous, imaginative answer to those questions. In fact, that door is a magical portal to a rust-belt factory called Monsters, Inc., home to an assembly line of bedroom doors through which “scarers,” aka the boogey man, will pass, monsters such as James P. Sullivan (John Goodman), aka Sulley, a huge purple and green furry guy, and his sidekick buddy, Mike Warkowski (Billy Crystal), who is a one-eyed, lime-green dude with a huge mouth. Their mission is to scare those children hiding under the covers, bottle their scream, and then return through the designated door where they use the harvested energy from the frightened scream to run the town of Monsteropolis. The only problem is that kids are not as easily frightened as they used to be, hence there’s less energy to run the factory. And so begins the story, with a small, pugnacious toddler who somehow slips through her closet door and finds herself in the Monster, Inc. factory where she is discovered by Sulley. Her presence triggers the CDA (Child Detection Agency) alarm, triggering a search by CDA agents. Luckily, she is rescued by Sulley, who calls her “Boo,” and manages to smuggle her out of the factory in a bag. Sulley and Mike make it their mission to return Boo back to her home. But first the two have to find Boo’s magical closet door, which is somewhere down on the factory floor. Meanwhile, Boo is in danger of being subjected to the Scream Extractor. And thus begins Sulley and Mike’s adventure as they deal with their nemesis Randal Boggs (Steve Buscemi), a monster who competes with the duo for the most scares, and behind conspires with Henry I. Waternoose III, C.E.O. of the factory, their purpose being to undermine Sulley and Mike. Monsters, Inc. has lots of twists and turns – at one point, the dynamic duo end up in the Himalayas and are taken in by an abdominal snowman, but soon make their way back to the factory. And they still have to get Boo home. It’s all good fun, and kids will more than enjoy the gags and antics of Mike and Sulley, who are never scary, just outrageously enjoyable to hang out with. Plus, the story has a satisfying ending wherein Sulley takes over Waternoose’s job as C.E.O. and retools the factory to use children’s laughter, not screams, to provide energy for Monster, Inc. and the Monsteropolis. Monsters, Inc. Pixar Animation. Directed by Pete Docter. 1 hr., 32 min. Rated G. A scene from Pixar’s Monsters, Inc.

Last Wednesday was another beautiful day for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. The morning clouds had cleared and the air quality was much improved. This lovely late summer morning brought out a strong turnout of 30 walkers at the Exedra. Two weeks earlier during a walking tour of Julia Morgan homes conducted by Will Adams, Jay Russell, the Post’s Question Man reporter, asked some walkers what unique piece of Piedmont history they have learned from their walks. One response was that early Piedmont philanthropist Wallace Alexander made some very significant contributions to Piedmont, but he does not get the recognition that he deserves. The group was interested in learning more about Alexander and seeing what he and his family created. Drawing on information in Gail Lombardi’s Piedmont Historical Society articles in the Post, the group learned that Alexander’s contributions were many. First, he was instrumental in the construction of Piedmont’s commercial center. In 1916 Alexander also arranged for the purchase of the land for the Piedmont Interdenominational Church, now the Piedmont Community Church. He hired Albert Farr, the architect who designed much of the center of Piedmont, for this project. Alexander then arranged for the purchase in 1921 of two acres of upper Piedmont Park land from the widow of Frank C. Havens, saving it from development. Additionally, Alexander established the Piedmont Boy Scout Council in 1921. Wallace Alexander was born in Maui in 1869. His family was a leader in the creation of the Hawaiian sugar industry. However, the family moved to the Bay Area so that Wallace and his sisters could attend school in Oakland. He married his Oakland High School classmate, Mary Baker, in 1904, and they chose a large site on the corner of Sea View and Hampton Avenues. They built a three-story mansion that they named “Brown Gables” for its large, brown painted dormers. There was also a carriage house to the west on what is now King Avenue. The Alexanders created a bit of a family community in this area. In 1911 Alexander’s mother built her own home at 92 Sea View across the street from Brown Gables, and Mary’s mother built a home further down the street at 236 Sea View. These homes are still there, but Brown Gables no longer exists. After Alexander died from a stroke in 1939, his wife followed his wish that the mansion be torn down, and the land subdivided into 13 lots that were sold, so that more families could live in Piedmont. The walkers decided to make his creations their destinations for the day. The first was easy. Across Highland Avenue from the Exedra are relatively new real estate and bank offices on the commercial site that Alexander once helped build. The group started up Mountain Avenue where they admired Alexander and Farr’s Piedmont Community Church. The walkers climbed a little over half a mile up Mountain to Sea View Avenue, where they went in search of the edge of Alexander’s estate, which ran from what is now 83 Sea View to Hampton Avenue. They stopped for a photo in front of 92 Sea View, Alexander’s mother’s beautiful home. The walkers saw tiles inlaid in the sidewalk spelling “Kailani,” a message left by the Alexanders as a reminder of their original Hawaii home. The walkers crossed Hampton and continued on Sea View to see the home of Mary’s mother. They also noted the Julia Morgan designed home they had seen a couple of weeks before. The group went on Farragut Avenue, passing more Julia Morgan homes that they recognized from their earlier walk. articles.text: On Monday night, August 30, Piedmont Police received a call at 6:34 p.m. about two people fighting in the parking lot at Ace Hardware on Grand Avenue. A man and woman were reportedly hitting each other with bottles and yelling at each other. A description of the subjects’ vehicle, a silver 2000 Honda Civic, matched that from a call 20 minutes earlier about a vehicle stolen from Alta Avenue. When the police arrived, the reporting person informed the police that the couple left in a silver Civic and left behind a vehicle without plates, a blue 2001 Acura TL which was also potentially involved in the Alta Avenue car theft. The reporting person also identified a third person who was in the silver car and walked away from the scene. Officers located the third person, Devante Sanders, (29 years old from Oakland) on Grand Avenue. He was on parole with a full search clause. A search revealed three shaved car keys and a glass pipe for narcotics. He was arrested and taken to Santa Rita jail. While officers were having the blue Acura towed, the female suspect returned to the parking lot to attempt to take the car. Lilyanna Ramos (25 years old from Oakland) had a warrant for driving with a suspended license. She was also arrested and taken to Santa Rita jail for the outstanding warrant and possession of a stolen vehicle. One male suspect involved in the car theft is still at large. Anyone with information about the suspect is encouraged to contact Piedmont Detective John Lagios at 420-3000.
